title: 21 Things You Should Never Do To Students
author: Michael Linsin
summary: Linsin argues that effective classroom management is as much about what teachers refrain from doing as what they actively do, framing the removal of harmful habits as capable of profoundly improving behavior while simplifying teachers' lives. He lists 21 specific practices to avoid entirely, including rewarding good behavior, scolding, praising expected behavior, arguing with students, reflection forms, behavior contracts, token systems, and punishing the whole class for a few students' actions. He notes that although many of these are common, even standard, teaching practices, they are nonetheless harmful to students and classrooms. He directs readers to the site's archive for the reasoning behind each item, since all but one have been covered extensively elsewhere. The piece closes by framing the removal of these 21 practices as a path to a calmer, more effective, and easier teaching life.
points: Effective classroom management is framed as being as much about eliminating harmful habits as about adding positive strategies.

Linsin acknowledges many of these practices are common, even standard, in classrooms today, yet still argues they are harmful.
Readers are pointed to the site archive for detailed reasoning behind each item on the list.
Removing these 21 practices is presented as a path toward reduced stress, greater effectiveness, and a calmer classroom.
quotes: Effective classroom management is as much about what you don’t do. As it is about what you do .
The removal of common but ultimately hurtful strategies . . . Can have a profound impact on behavior.
In that spirit, and truth, what follows are 21 things you should never do to students. Ever, ever, ever.
The whys and hows of all 21—except #16, which we’ll cover in a future article—have been written about extensively on this website.
In the meantime, although many of the “never dos” listed above are common teaching practice, make no mistake. They’re bad for students and bad for your classroom.
Removing them from your classroom management toolkit will put you far ahead of the curve. It will make you more effective and more influential and bring a natural calm to your class.
